sections.title: Conditional Probability
sections.content: The probability of event A given that event B has already occurred is P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B). Multiplication theorem: P(A ∩ B) = P(B) * P(A|B).

sections.title: Law of Total Probability & Bayes' Theorem
sections.content: Total Probability: P(A) = Σ [P(E_i) * P(A|E_i)]. Bayes' Theorem reverses the condition: P(E_1|A) = [P(E_1) * P(A|E_1)] / [Σ P(E_i) * P(A|E_i)]. It finds the probability of a specific 'cause' given the 'effect'.

sections.title: Effect of Shifting and Scaling on Stats
sections.content: If every observation is multiplied by 'a' and 'b' is added (y = ax + b): New Mean = a*(Old Mean) + b. New Variance = a² * (Old Variance). New SD = |a| * (Old SD). Note: Adding/subtracting does NOT change Variance or SD.

sections.title: Coefficient of Variation (CV)
sections.content: CV = (Standard Deviation / Mean) * 100. It is a unitless measure used to compare the consistency of two different data sets. A lower CV indicates higher consistency (less variability).

sections.title: Tautology and Fallacy
sections.content: A Tautology is a logical statement that is ALWAYS True regardless of the truth values of its components (e.g., p ∨ ~p). A Fallacy (or Contradiction) is ALWAYS False (e.g., p ∧ ~p).

sections.title: Converse, Inverse, and Contrapositive
sections.content: For a conditional statement p → q: Converse is q → p. Inverse is ~p → ~q. Contrapositive is ~q → ~p. Crucial Rule: A statement and its Contrapositive are logically equivalent.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
1) Confusing the Converse with the Contrapositive in logic questions.
2) Adding the constant 'b' to the new Variance when data is shifted (Variance only scales with a²).
3) In Bayes' Theorem, forgetting to add all the possible mutually exclusive paths in the denominator.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 2 handles heavily tested JEE concepts: Bayes' theorem (reverse probability), how data scaling strictly affects variance, and identifying logical equivalences through Contrapositives.

tricks.title: Implication Equivalence Trick
tricks.explanation: The statement p → q is logically exactly equivalent to ~p ∨ q. This is the most frequently tested logic equivalence in JEE.
tricks.example: 'If it rains (p), I carry an umbrella (q)' is equivalent to 'It does not rain (~p) OR I carry an umbrella (q)'.

tricks.title: Negation of Implication
tricks.explanation: The negation of (p → q) is NOT (~p → ~q). Using the equivalence trick, ~(~p ∨ q) applies De Morgan's to become (p ∧ ~q).
tricks.example: Negation of 'If I study, I pass' is 'I study AND I do not pass'.

tricks.title: Bayes' Theorem Tree Diagram
tricks.explanation: Don't memorize the massive formula. Draw a tree diagram. The required probability is just: (The specific path branch product) / (Sum of ALL path branch products leading to the outcome).
tricks.example: Path A / (Path A + Path B + Path C).

tricks.title: Variance of First n Natural Numbers
tricks.explanation: Memorize this direct formula to save calculation time. The variance of 1, 2, 3, ..., n is exactly (n² - 1) / 12.

tricks.title: Mean Deviation Shortcut for A.P.
tricks.explanation: The Mean Deviation about the mean for an Arithmetic Progression with 'n' terms and common difference 'd' is [n*d/4] if n is even, and [(n²-1)d / 4n] if n is odd.
tricks.example: Saves finding the mean and subtracting it from every term manually.

tricks.title: Conditional Probability Venn Trick
tricks.explanation: To find P(A|B), temporarily ignore the whole sample space. Treat B as your NEW sample space. The answer is just the intersection area divided by area of B.
tricks.example: If A=spades, B=black cards. P(Spades | Black) = 13 spades / 26 black cards = 1/2.
